Well, Doc, it is a whole big fuss over nothing if you ask me, but my family insisted I come see you. You see, it all goes back to the county fair this past weekend. I always give a talk there. Have for years. Mostly about soil management and equipment, seeing as I’ve been running the ranch since I got out of high school. It is a good crowd usually, folks who really care about the land. 

Anyway, I was right in the middle of my presentation by the equipment showcase, and I just realized that I needed to show them the new pattern. Not just talk about it, because words do not do it justice, I had to really demonstrate it. So I climbed right up onto this big tractor they had on display—beautiful machine, really, heavy duty—and I got up in the cab and started jerking the controls around. I was pulling the levers this way and that, yanking them to show the crowd exactly how the new pattern works, how the angles all line up and make sense. 

And then people started yelling. The fairgrounds people, my family, they were all hollering at me to get down and stop messing with the machinery. But I just... I couldn't make myself stop. Even with everyone yelling at me and waving their arms, my hands just kept jerking those controls because the crowd needed to see the pattern, and I had to finish showing them. So, they eventually pulled me down from the cab and, well, that is why they brought me in today.

Well, now that you mention it, Doc... I suppose there is something else. And I haven't really talked about it much because, well, folks around here don't always understand the land the way I do. I'll be standing there, maybe leaning on my shovel, just listening to them tell me exactly how the land is doing.

Like I was just saying, Doc—and I know you probably have a checklist there and have to ask these things twice just to make absolutely sure you got it all down right in your notes—but the answer is still no. There's too much at stake, too much that relies on me being sharp and paying attention to the land and the animals. You see, when you run a ranch, there is no such thing as a nine-to-five. The fences don't mend themselves, the livestock doesn't wait for you to finish your morning coffee, and the weather certainly doesn't care if you're tired. But I suppose... if you mean this specific feeling, this real charged-up feeling where I just keep going and going? It’s been a good long stretch. \n\nI was actually thinking about this the other day when I was out checking the south perimeter wire. I realized I haven't really been needing to sleep much at all lately. I'll just lay there in bed feeling like a tractor engine running on idle, just humming, waiting for the sun to come up so I can get back out there and work. Honestly, these charged, sleepless, nonstop stretches... they have taken up about ten months of this past year or so. \n\nTen solid months! I mean, it started way back before the winter thaw, right around the time I decided to completely overhaul the irrigation setup in the lower pasture. My boys told me to wait for spring, but I had the energy, I had the vision for how the pipes needed to route, and I just couldn't stop working on it. Day and night, night and day. My wife kept coming out to the barn telling me to come inside and rest, but why on earth would I rest when I don't even feel tired? When your mind is just firing on all cylinders and you can see exactly how the whole property connects together, you don't just go to sleep. You use that energy. So yeah, about ten months out of the last year, just nonstop pushing through. I really don't see the problem with a man being highly productive, to be perfectly honest with you, but I guess that's what my family is in such a twist about.\n\nDoctor: During this period, have you had any experiences like hearing or seeing things other people couldn’t, or feeling that someone was controlling your thoughts or actions?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you mention it, Doc... I suppose there is something else. And I haven't really talked about it much because, well, folks around here don't always understand the land the way I do. You see, I've got this section out by the north pasture. It's a tricky piece of ground, always has been, ever since my granddad first cleared it. The soil there is a bit more alkaline, and the runoff from the ridge makes it a real puzzle to manage. \n\nAnyway, especially near dusk—you know that time of day when the shadows get long and the light turns all golden and heavy?—I'll be out there checking the irrigation lines. I put in those new PVC lines a few years back to try and get better coverage, but lately... lately, when I'm walking those rows, I hear these voices. Well, like I was telling you before, Doc—and I don't mind repeating myself if it helps you get the full picture, because I know it's a lot to take in—but yes, absolutely. Two weeks, three weeks, even longer. There was that whole stretch last fall, like I mentioned. I'd be walking along the fence line, checking the tension on the barbed wire, and I'd hear the lines talking to me, clear as day. They'd be whispering across the frost, telling me things about the soil, about the water table. And in the evenings, when I'd sit down at the kitchen table with a bowl of stew and the farm data printouts from the extension office—just sitting there calm as could be, not a racing thought in my head—I still saw the hidden warnings in those numbers. I still knew, without a doubt, exactly what the data was really saying about the poisoned rows. 

So it's not just when my engine is running hot, Doc. Not at all. Those voices, those messages in the data... they stick around for weeks at a time, even when I'm just living my quiet, everyday life, not energized or grand in the slightest. The land speaks when it speaks, and it doesn't wait for me to be fired up to do it.

Now Doc, I gotta ask... is your pen out of ink? Because I feel like we are plowing the exact same field three times over today. I know you doctors have your clipboards and your checklists and you gotta be real thorough, but I swear I just answered this for you twice already.

Oh, absolutely they do. It's like... well, think of it like turning up the pressure valve on a main water line. The harder the pump runs, the louder the whole system rattles. 

Take that big push I did a while back. During those months when I was sleeping hardly at all—I mean, maybe two hours a night, just dozing in the armchair with my boots still on because my mind was racing with too much work to do—I was pushing the farm expansion day and night. I'd be out there at three in the morning, walking the new property lines in the pitch black, and I was hearing those voices in the irrigation lines so loud and clear, just echoing right through the aluminum pipes. It wasn't just a quiet whisper like in the fall, it was... it was urgent. It was everywhere. 

And then I'd march back into the kitchen, lay out all the historical yield maps on the table, and I was reading warnings in those maps that were practically jumping off the paper at me. The patterns were so intense, showing me exactly where the soil was turning sour and what I had to do to stop it. 

So, yes. When my engine is revved up and I've got that kind of energy pushing me, all of it—the voices, the messages in the data—it all just ramps right up alongside it. You can't separate the two when I'm in that mode, they just feed right into each other and it all feels bigger.

Well... yeah. Yes, I have. I suppose I can't hide that from you since it's probably stamped in big red letters in whatever file you've got sitting there anyway. But let me explain how that actually went down, because if you just read the intake forms, you're not getting the full picture of what was actually happening.

And because I run a pretty sizable operation, they usually ask me to give a little talk or a demonstration on the main stage area—usually about equipment upgrades or soil conservation, something straightforward. 

So this one year, I was scheduled to speak, and I was right in the middle of one of those stretches I just told you about. I was buzzing. I was supposed to give a standard ten-minute talk on some new machinery. But when I got up to the microphone... I looked out at all those folks sitting on the bleachers, eating their funnel cakes, and I realized just talking at them wasn't going to be enough. Words weren't going to cut it. I had to show them.

I was jerking those controls so hard the whole cab was shaking, and the crowd started murmuring, and then people started yelling at me to get down. I just couldn't make myself stop, even with all those people yelling at me. It was like I was locked in, like my hands were glued to the levers and I absolutely had to finish showing them the pattern no matter what. 

Eventually, they had to get the sheriff's deputies and the EMTs to come physically pull me down off that tractor. And they didn't let my wife take me home, Doc. They put me in the back of the ambulance right there next to the prize-winning pumpkins and brought me straight in to be admitted. So... yes. That's how I ended up in the hospital.

Well, now... if you mean times when the engine isn't running hot, when I'm just... well, just going about my business like a regular fellow... yes. Yes, there have been times exactly like that. 

You see, farming isn't always go, go, go. You've got your dead seasons. Take late November or December, after the harvest is in the bins and the ground starts to freeze up hard. There's a stretch there, usually a good three, maybe four weeks, where things get real quiet around the property. The irrigation pipes, even when they were drained out for the winter, they'd still be echoing those same voices, plain as day, just whispering right to me while I worked. 

And then I'd go back inside, take my boots off, sit down at my desk with a regular cup of coffee—feeling completely level, no rushing thoughts, no buzzing in my veins at all—and I'd pull up the farm data on the computer just to do some end-of-year bookkeeping. And right there on the screen, I still saw it. I still completely believed that the farm data was carrying those hidden warnings. I could still read the threats about the poisoned rows right there in the spreadsheets. It didn't matter one bit that I wasn't wound up or running hot. The warnings were still there, and the voices were still there, day in and day out, for weeks on end, even when I was just sitting quietly by the woodstove.

Well, yes, Doc, that's... that's exactly what I was just trying to explain to you. I feel like maybe we're going around in circles here a bit, but I'll lay it out again because it's important you understand the timeline of how this all works on the farm.
